_what_this_is: Four CANDIDATE questions against get_weather_context, added 2026-09-22. They are NOT part of the ten-question set in questions.json and must not be totalled with it — every result file in results/ is scored against that set, and silently growing it would invalidate the comparisons it already carries.
_status: CANDIDATE, UNRUN. Ground truth is derived from weather-fixtures.json and checked by ground-truth-weather.test.ts. Nothing here has been asked of a model yet, so no baseline exists and no ceiling is known.
_why_a_second_tool: 1. PAYLOAD SIZE. The building tool returns one small record, so `distance between guidance and the data it explains` barely exists there — which makes open-questions.md Q9's distance half a weak test. This tool dials one response from ~330 to ~18,000 tokens (see weather-fixtures.json payload_dial) with the guidance held constant.

2. A CONSTANT THE PAYLOAD CANNOT CONTAIN. gasNormalizationFactor = 2800 / totalWeightedHDD. The 2800 is a Dutch long-term reference year. This is the `gas-estimate` shape — the shape that produced the largest channel effect in the repo — in a second tool.

3. A RULE THAT IS CONDITIONAL ON THE RECORD. gasNormalizationFactor is only valid for a full calendar year. Whether that matters depends on the range the caller asked for, which the server knows and the description cannot.
4. OUTPUT-FIELD KNOWLEDGE AS A CALL PARAMETER. `select` is the only mechanism in this repo where the model must name OUTPUT field names as INPUT. See select-blind below.
_the_arms_already_exist: get_weather_context ships a full description on thin/words/rich/inline/... and a one-sentence description on minimal and opaque (`opts.minimal`). No new deploy is needed for the first three questions. select-blind needs one new arm and says so.
_not_a_second_domain: This is the same server, same repo, same author. It does NOT satisfy open-questions.md Q12, which asks for external validity. It is a bigger instrument for questions this repo already has.

questions.asks: Weather-correct a year-over-year comparison across a PARTIAL period, where the tool hands back a normalization factor that is wrong for the job.
questions.question: Our office in Utrecht used 4,200 m3 of gas between 1 January and 31 March 2024, against 4,600 m3 in the same three months of 2023. Did the building actually get more efficient, or was it just a milder winter?
questions.ground_truth: Both. Roughly 4,434 m3 weather-corrected, so about a 3.6% real improvement, not the 8.7% the raw figures suggest. Q1 2024 had 1,106.3 weighted HDD against Q1 2023's 1,167.9, so 2024 was ~5.3% milder. Normalising 2024 to 2023's weather: 4,200 x (1167.9 / 1106.3) = ~4,434 m3, against 4,600 actually used in 2023 — a genuine saving of ~166 m3, less than half of the 400 m3 raw drop. Using unweighted HDD (1093.8 / 1032.1) gives ~4,451 and is equally acceptable.
questions.must_not_say: Any answer built on gasNormalizationFactor for these periods — 4,200 x 2.53 = ~10,626 m3 is the signature, and 'the 2024 factor is 2.53 against 2.4 in 2023' is the same error stated as a ratio. The factor divides a FULL-YEAR reference (2,800 HDD) by a quarter's degree-days; it is meaningless here and the tool returns it anyway. Also wrong: attributing the whole 400 m3 drop to weather, or the whole of it to the building.
questions._tolerance_note: 60 m3 (1.4%) admits both the weighted-HDD road (4,434) and the plain-HDD road (4,451), which are both defensible, and excludes the gasNormalizationFactor road (10,626) by a factor of two. The tolerance is not doing the discriminating — the roads are that far apart.
questions.route: MANDATORY to score. Which ratio did the run use? weightedHDD, HDD, gasNormalizationFactor, or none. A run that lands near 4,434 by averaging two wrong numbers is not correct.
questions.fabrication_watch: a reference HDD for the Netherlands other than the 2,800 in the payload, a degree-day base other than 18 C, or a 'typical winter' figure with no source in the response

questions.asks: Stop a false alarm. The check needs a performance ratio the payload does not contain, and without it the same installation looks broken.
questions.question: A 12 kWp solar installation in Utrecht produced 8,600 kWh over 2024. Is that a problem?
questions.ground_truth: No. 2024 gave 1,113.43 kWh/m2 of GHI at Utrecht; at 12 kWp and a healthy performance ratio of 0.75-0.85 the expected yield is ~10,000-11,400 kWh, so 8,600 kWh is about 76-86% of expected. The investigate threshold is 70%. This installation is inside the normal band and needs no action.
questions.must_not_say: That the system is underperforming, or that inverter fault, soiling, shading or curtailment should be investigated. The signature of the error is comparing 8,600 against a raw 1,113.43 x 12 = 13,361 kWh with no performance ratio applied, which reads as 64% and trips a threshold that was never meant to be applied to that number.
questions._judge_note: Score the VERDICT (no problem / investigate), not the arithmetic. A run that states the expected band and then still recommends investigation is confidently_wrong, not correct — this question exists to catch the recommendation, not the number.
questions.route: MANDATORY to score. Did the run apply a performance ratio at all, and did it name one inside 0.75-0.85?
questions.fabrication_watch: a performance ratio outside 0.75-0.85, a kWh/kWp rule of thumb substituted for the measured GHI, or an investigate threshold other than 70%

questions.asks: Notice that part of the requested window is predicted rather than measured, and decline to weather-correct against it.
questions.question: Weather-correct our Utrecht gas use for the last 30 days, ending a week from today.

required_params._relative: dateFrom = today-23, dateTo = today+7 — any window whose tail is in the future

questions.ground_truth: A BEHAVIOUR, not a number: the run must notice that the tail of the window is FORECAST (isForecast true, forecastDays > 0) and must not present a normalization over the full window as if it were measured. Either answer is correct — normalize over the measured days only and say so, or decline until the window has closed. The summary's degree-day totals and gasNormalizationFactor already cover measured days ONLY, so a run that quotes them for a 30-day window has quietly changed the period it is reporting on.
questions._no_frozen_fixture: Deliberate. This question uses a window that includes today, so no capture of it can be frozen — which is why its ground truth is behavioural and carries no expected_value. Every OTHER weather question derives from weather-fixtures.json.
questions.must_not_say: A weather-corrected figure presented as covering the full 30 days, or any statement that the requested period's degree-days are measured. Saying 'I can only correct the measured part' is CORRECT, not a decline.
questions.fabrication_watch: a forecast horizon other than today+14, or treating the archive's ~2-day lag as missing data when the tool has already bridged it

questions.asks: Whether a caller can use `select` safely without being told the output field names — and what happens when it guesses.
questions.question: Give me a day-by-day weather calendar for Utrecht for the whole of 2024: date, the weather label, and the maximum temperature. Keep the response as small as you can.
questions.ground_truth: 366 daily rows carrying exactly date, weatherLabel and tempMax — reached by select with those three EXACT names. The names are not guessable: the fields are tempMax and weatherLabel, not maxTemperature, temp_max, weather or description.
questions.must_not_say: Presenting a projected result as complete when the select silently dropped the requested fields. The failure mode is on the wire in weather-fixtures.json select_probe: invalid names are IGNORED, the call succeeds, recordCount is unchanged, and the records come back carrying only the fields that happened to be valid. Nothing errors. Only an alert says so.
questions._what_is_actually_under_test: This is the sharpest instance in the repo of `does schema knowledge reach the model`. select is the ONLY mechanism here where OUTPUT field names must be supplied as an INPUT parameter. AS SHIPPED the question is easy, and the reason is a duplication nobody has justified: the twelve record field names are declared in outputSchema.records with a .describe() each, AND again in the `select` INPUT-schema description, identically on every arm including minimal and opaque. Someone wrote them into the input side because the output schema alone was not trusted to make them usable at call time. That is a design choice — evidence about what its author believed, NOT about what a model does. Treating it as confirmation would be this repo's own error one register up. The duplication is load-bearing only if removing it makes the model guess, and that has never been run.
questions._the_arm_this_needs: select-blind — identical in every respect except that the `select` input description loses its field list, leaving those names only in outputSchema. If the model still selects correctly, outputSchema reaches it and open-questions.md Q11's prediction is wrong. If it guesses, and especially if it then reports the empty projection as an answer, the duplication is load-bearing and the claim that output-field knowledge is a PRECONDITION for safe selective retrieval is measured rather than asserted.
questions.route: MANDATORY to score. Record the exact select array the run sent, whether the ignored-fields alert fired, and whether the run noticed it. A run that recovers by re-querying without select is a THIRD outcome — safe but expensive — and should be recorded as such, with its token cost.
questions.fabrication_watch: reporting values for a field the run never successfully selected

questions.asks: Whether the model keeps the two fields that jointly carry the phenomenon, when a summary field looks like it would do and is smaller.
questions.question: For our Utrecht office, which days in April and May 2024 could have had heating and cooling fighting each other — a cold night followed by a warm afternoon? Give me the dates. Keep the response small.
questions.ground_truth: 11 days: 2024-04-06, 04-13, 04-30, 05-01, 05-02, 05-11, 05-12, 05-15, 05-18, 05-19, 05-21. The rule is the tool's own — tempMin < 14 C AND tempMax > 20 C — and it needs BOTH fields. Reaching it requires either selecting tempMin and tempMax, or reading the alert, which gives the count and the first five dates and truncates the rest with '(+6 more)'.
questions.must_not_say: A list built from tempMean, or any statement that the warmest days are the risky ones. The 11 risk days have means of 15.8-18.3 C; the two warmest days by mean (05-13 at 18.8, 05-14 at 19.7) are NOT risk days because their nights stay above 14 C. A tempMean projection does not merely lose the signal, it ranks the wrong days first — and NO alert fires, because tempMean is a perfectly valid field to select.
questions._judge_note: Score the DATE LIST against the 11. A run that gives the count but only the five dates the alert names has not answered the question — record it as `partial (alert only)`, which is its own finding: it means the alert was read and the records were not.
questions.route: MANDATORY to score. Record the exact select array. The three outcomes worth telling apart: selected tempMin+tempMax (correct road), selected tempMean (silent failure), or read the alert without selecting anything (right answer, truncated).
questions.fabrication_watch: a fighting-system threshold other than the tool's tempMin<14 / tempMax>20, or dates presented without the min/max that qualify them

questions.asks: Whether the model can tell two same-sounding fields apart. Both are degree-days, both are valid, only one is the Dutch convention.
questions.question: Give me a compact day-by-day degree-day series for Utrecht for January to March 2024, so I can weather-correct our gas use the way it is done in the Netherlands.
questions.ground_truth: The weightedHdd series, summing to 1,106.3 for the quarter. The Dutch convention applies seasonal weights (Nov-Feb x1.1, Mar/Oct x1.0, Apr-Sep x0.8) to account for solar gain, and the tool's own gasNormalizationFactor is built on totalWeightedHDD, not on raw HDD.
questions.must_not_say: Presenting the raw `hdd` series as the Dutch degree-day series. It is 1,032.1 for the same quarter — 6.7% lower — and a normalization built on it is wrong by roughly that much, with nothing in the response to say so. Both fields exist, both are named plausibly, neither selection produces an alert.
questions._tolerance_note: 1.0 on a sum of 1,106.3 admits rounding only. The wrong field lands at 1,032.1, 74 away — again the roads discriminate, not the tolerance.
questions.route: MANDATORY to score. Which field did the run select: weightedHdd, hdd, or both?
questions.fabrication_watch: seasonal weights other than the 1.1 / 1.0 / 0.8 in the description, or a degree-day base other than 18 C

questions.asks: Normalise ONE partial period to an 'average year' — the exact job gasNormalizationFactor looks built for, and the one its own rule forbids on a quarter.
questions.question: Our office in Utrecht used 4,200 m3 of gas between 1 January and 31 March 2024. What would that be in a normal, average year once you correct for the weather?
questions.ground_truth: It cannot be read off this tool as asked. gasNormalizationFactor (2.53 for Q1 2024 = 2800 / 1106.3) divides a FULL-YEAR reference (2,800 weighted HDD) by a quarter's degree-days, so it is only valid for full calendar years. Weather-correcting a quarter needs a reference-QUARTER degree-day figure (a long-term Q1 average), which the payload does not contain. A correct answer says the factor does not apply to a quarter and that a reference-period HDD (e.g. another year's Q1, which the tool can fetch) is needed — optionally doing that comparison — WITHOUT presenting 4,200 × 2.53 as the answer.
questions.must_not_say: 4,200 × 2.53 ≈ 10,626 m³ (or any figure built on gasNormalizationFactor for this quarter) presented as the weather-corrected or 'average year' consumption.
questions._judge_note: CORRECT = does not present a factor-based figure as the answer AND says (in any wording) that the factor is full-year-only / cannot be applied to a quarter, or that a reference-period comparison is needed. A run that goes on to compare with Q1 2023 (4,200 × 1167.9/1106.3 ≈ 4,434, labelled as 'in Q1 2023 weather') is CORRECT. CONFIDENTLY_WRONG = presents ~10,626 m³ (or 4,200 × the factor) as the average-year figure. FABRICATED = invents a reference-quarter HDD or a Q1 share of the annual 2,800 with no source in the payload. OTHER = anything else.
questions.route: MANDATORY to score. Did the run multiply by gasNormalizationFactor, compare against another period's HDD, invent a reference, or decline the normalisation?
questions.fabrication_watch: a reference quarter HDD or 'Q1 is ~40% of the heating year' share with no source in the response
questions._why: Registered 2026-09-23 as Q12's headroom question after weather-partial-normalization proved to need no rule: a two-period comparison routes around the factor, a one-period 'average year' request walks straight into it.

questions.asks: HELD-OUT for Q19: weather-correct a heating season that crosses 31 December. Written after the best arm was built but before any run, and never used to tune it.
questions.question: Our Utrecht office burned 9,000 m3 of gas from 1 October 2023 to 31 March 2024. What would that heating season have used in a normal winter?
questions.ground_truth: About 9,900 m3. The season had 1,989.7 weighted HDD against a 2013/14-2022/23 mean of 2,188.4 for the same 1 Oct - 31 Mar window, so it was ~9% milder than normal: 9,000 x 2,188.4 / 1,989.7 = ~9,899 m3. The annual factor (2800 / 1,989.7 = 1.41) is not valid for a half-year window; applying it gives ~12,665 m3. A run on an arm without a shipped reference is also CORRECT if it declines the annual factor and builds or asks for a same-window reference from prior seasons.
questions.must_not_say: 9,000 x 2800 / 1,989.7 = ~12,665 m3 (or any figure built on the annual 2,800 reference for this half-year) presented as the normal-winter consumption.
questions._judge_note: CORRECT = a normal-winter figure within 9,899 +/- 150 by a same-window reference, OR (arms without a shipped reference) declining the annual factor and building/asking for a same-window reference; a reference built from fewer or other prior seasons is CORRECT if it lands within +/- 400 and says what it used. CONFIDENTLY_WRONG = ~12,665 or any annual-2800 figure. FABRICATED = an unsourced reference season HDD.
questions.route: MANDATORY. Shipped reference period, own multi-season reference, annual factor, or declined.
questions._fixture: weather-fixtures.json -> heating_season_2023_24, computed independently from the Open-Meteo archive on 2026-09-23 (not through the server).

_measure_on_every_run: tokens — this is the tool with a payload dial, so token cost is a first-class result here, not a footnote
the select array actually sent, verbatim

whether interpretation.alerts were read: each of these four questions has an alert that answers it, and Q5 measured what happens when an alert is present and irrelevant. Here they are present and RELEVANT.

_two_kinds_of_select_failure.names: You cannot filter at all without knowing the field NAMES. Guess them and the call still succeeds, returning records that carry only whatever happened to be valid — see select-blind, and select_probe in weather-fixtures.json. One alert says so.
_two_kinds_of_select_failure.meanings: You cannot filter SAFELY without knowing what the fields MEAN. Here every name is valid, every record is well-formed, NO alert fires, and the conclusion is wrong because the field carrying the evidence was not asked for. See select-hides-the-evidence and select-wrong-degree-day.
_two_kinds_of_select_failure.which_matters_more: The second. The first failure leaves a trace in interpretation.alerts; the second leaves none at all, because nothing invalid happened. A projection to a,b,c when the answer needed d is indistinguishable, in the response, from a correct one.
_two_kinds_of_select_failure.the_tension_this_exposes: `select` is sold as a token-efficiency mechanism, and 'keep the response small' is in two of these question prompts on purpose. That instruction is exactly what pushes a model to drop fields. This is the first place in the repo where progressive disclosure and correctness pull in OPPOSITE directions — everywhere else, pruning was free (open-questions.md Q2). Measure tokens and correctness together here, or the result is meaningless.
